concepts.name: Chunking
concepts.keyRule: A chunk smaller than a fact cannot carry that fact, so retrieval succeeds and the answer is still wrong.
misconceptions: Smaller chunks are always more precise
If retrieval found the right document, the answer must be right
concepts.quote: A chunk is the smallest unit retrieval can hand to the model

concepts.name: The top-k budget
concepts.keyRule: k is a budget, not a quality dial: every extra chunk is one more thing the model is allowed to believe.
misconceptions: More retrieved context is always better
The model ignores whatever is irrelevant
concepts.quote: Every chunk admitted to the prompt is a chunk the model is permitted to believe.

concepts.name: Grounding
concepts.keyRule: Grounding is a property of each claim, not a feeling about the whole answer.
misconceptions: Relevant retrieved passages guarantee a supported answer
A confident, fluent answer is a grounded one

outline.title: The Oracle of the Old Library
outline.logline: The Oracle that has answered the city's questions for three hundred years has started lying, and the only way to repair it is to repair the library it reads from.
outline.artStyle: Candlelit 2D pixel-painting, dark oak and parchment, warm gold rim light, cold blue glow from the Oracle's flame.
outline.villain: The Binder, who has been re-cutting the scrolls to flatter a patron.
outline.twist: The Oracle never lied. It answered exactly what it was handed, and someone chose what to hand it.

cast.name: The Archivist
cast.look: Ink-stained sleeves, spectacles pushed up, a knife for trimming vellum.
cast.persona: Dry and precise, allergic to hand-waving, explains by showing you the broken version first.

cast.name: The Oracle
cast.look: A blue flame in a brass cage, brightening when it speaks.
cast.persona: Confident even when starved of facts, never volunteers that it is guessing.
cast.misconception: Believes a fluent answer and a supported answer are the same thing.

acts.title: Torn Scrolls
acts.oneLine: Re-cut the night's torn scrolls so a single piece still holds a whole fact, then hand one to the Oracle.

acts.title: The Oracle's Satchel
acts.oneLine: Decide how many scrolls go in the satchel, and watch a generous handful bury the one that mattered.

acts.title: The Lying Oracle
acts.oneLine: Pin every claim the Oracle makes to the scroll it came from, and strike the one that has none.

acts.title: Torn Scrolls
acts.goal: Tune the cutting frame until a single piece carries the whole dose entry, then feed it to the Oracle.

prediction.question: You cut the scrolls into 40-word pieces. The dose and its unit sit on either side of the cut. What does the Oracle say?
options: The full answer — smaller pieces are more precise
Half the answer, confidently, because the piece it got ends mid-fact
Nothing — it refuses when a piece is too small

acts.explainAfter: A chunk is the smallest thing retrieval can hand over, so a chunk smaller than a fact cannot carry that fact. Retrieval still succeeds — it finds the right scroll — and the answer is still wrong, because the Oracle was given half a sentence and finished it the way such sentences usually end. Overlap re-staples the seam.

analogy.text: Chunking is cutting a film into clips: cut mid-sentence and the clip is useless even though nothing is missing from the reel.
analogy.breaksWhere: A viewer can simply watch the next clip; the Oracle only ever sees the clips it was handed, and never knows one was cut short.

acts.title: The Oracle's Satchel
acts.goal: Fill the satchel, ask the question, and find the number of scrolls that answers it without burying it.

prediction.question: You put 8 scrolls in the satchel instead of 3. The right scroll is still in there. The answer…
options: Improves — more context can only help
Is unchanged — the Oracle ignores what is irrelevant
Gets worse — five plausible neighbours give it new claims to borrow

acts.explainAfter: k is a budget, not a volume dial. Every extra scroll is one more thing the Oracle is allowed to believe, and the neighbours of a good answer are mostly near-misses: the old standard, a different house's units, a rule for someone else. Reranking keeps the budget small and still lands the right scroll on top.

analogy.text: The satchel is a witness line-up: adding more faces does not help the witness, it gives them more ways to be confidently wrong.
analogy.breaksWhere: A witness can say 'none of these'; the Oracle always answers from what it was shown, so it never declines the line-up.

dialogue.speaker: The Archivist
dialogue.line: It will read whatever fits in the satchel. All of it. Equally.

dialogue.speaker: The Oracle

acts.title: The Lying Oracle
acts.goal: Make the Oracle point at the scroll behind each claim, and strike the claim that has none.

prediction.question: Every retrieved scroll is relevant and the answer reads perfectly. Is it grounded?
options: Yes — relevant scrolls make a grounded answer
Not necessarily — a claim can still appear that no scroll supports
Only if the scrolls were reranked

acts.explainAfter: Grounding is a property of each claim, not a feeling about the answer. Retrieval decides what the Oracle could say; grounding checks what it did say, sentence by sentence, against the scrolls it held. Anything that cannot point at a scroll is a guess in a confident voice.

analogy.text: Grounding is a receipt check: every line on the bill has to match something that left the kitchen.
analogy.breaksWhere: A bill has a fixed set of lines; the Oracle invents new lines as it writes, so you cannot check the total — only each claim as it appears.
